hey, so i joined this board game guild a couple months ago—the riverview tabletop guild? they have this one-page charter with membership tiers. section 4 says anyone who goes to five sanctioned weekend sessions in a rolling eight-week window gets active member status, which means voting rights on game purchases.

i kept track: june 1st, 8th, 15th, 22nd, and 29th. that's five straight weekends. but julian, the organizer, told me new members usually wait for an email invitation before they're considered active... which made me second-guess.

honestly, showing up five weeks in a row took some deliberate effort on my part, socially. i'm just wondering if the written charter means i qualify outright, or if i'm reading it wrong.

Short version: based on what you've described, you're not reading it wrong. Five sanctioned weekend sessions inside a rolling eight-week window is the test, and June 1–29 is five sessions spanning about four weeks. That clears the bar with room to spare.

A few things worth double-checking in the actual wording before you plant a flag, though, since I'm going off your summary rather than the document itself:

- **How does section 4 phrase the result?** "Becomes an active member" or "is granted active status" reads as automatic. "Is eligible for" or "may be designated" leaves room for a step where someone has to act on it. That one word matters a lot here.
- **Is "sanctioned" defined?** Usually it means something like "sessions listed on the official calendar" or "hosted by a guild officer." If any of those five weekends was a casual pickup night rather than an official session, it might not count.
- **Is there anything elsewhere in the charter about new members, probation periods, or dues?** A one-pager can still bury a "new members complete a 60-day intro period" line in section 2 that quietly modifies section 4.
- **Is there a notice or confirmation clause?** Sometimes the rule is "status takes effect upon confirmation by the membership coordinator," and the email is just that confirmation mechanism.

Julian's comment ("new members *usually* wait for an email") sounds like how things are administered in practice, not necessarily a rule. Those two things get blurred constantly in small volunteer clubs. The charter is what the group actually agreed to; the email may just be the habit that grew up around it. Quite possibly the email is the confirmation and nobody's gotten around to sending yours.

The clean move is to ask Julian directly and specifically, something like: "I read section 4 as five sanctioned sessions in eight weeks—I hit that on June 1, 8, 15, 22, and 29. Is the email just the confirmation step, or is there another requirement I'm missing?" That's not combative; it just asks him to point to the rule if one exists.

And for what it's worth, five straight weekends of showing up somewhere new, on purpose, when it doesn't come easy, is genuinely the hard part. The status question is a paperwork detail by comparison.

If you paste the charter text, I can read section 4 word-for-word and tell you whether the language is automatic or discretionary.

yeah that's fair, i should just paste the charter text. section 4 exactly: "any member who attends five (5) sanctioned weekend sessions within any rolling eight (8) week period shall be recognized as an active guild member, with corresponding voting privileges on library acquisitions."

sounds automatic, right? 'shall be recognized'... but then julian's comment about the email threw me. maybe i'm overthinking it 🤔

Yep, that's about as automatic as charter language gets. "Shall" is the mandatory word in this kind of document. "May be recognized" would give someone discretion; "shall be recognized" doesn't. Once the condition is met (five sanctioned sessions in eight weeks), the status follows.

One small nuance, which I think actually reconciles Julian's comment with the text: "shall be *recognized*" does imply somebody does the recognizing. So the most sensible reading is that the email is the guild's mechanism for that recognition, not a separate gate you have to pass. The charter doesn't say "upon invitation" or "at the organizer's discretion," so Julian can't withhold it, but he can be the one who formalizes it. That's probably all he meant: "we'll email you when we've marked you active," said a bit loosely.

The one thing that could still trip you is whether all five June dates were "sanctioned" sessions under whatever definition the charter uses. If they were on the official calendar or run by an officer, you're done.

So, not overthinking. You've met the requirement and the wording backs you up. Just close the loop: "Hey Julian, per section 4 I hit five sanctioned sessions on June 1, 8, 15, 22, and 29. Can you mark me active, or is there anything else needed?" Framing it as "can you process this" rather than "am I allowed" matches what the charter actually says.

hmm okay so "shall be recognized" is pretty definitive then. thanks for walking through that.

i think part of why his comment stuck with me was because showing up those five weeks genuinely was a lot for me, socially. like i planned my whole week around it each time. so hearing "oh you'll get an email eventually" felt a little deflating, like the effort didn't quite register.

anyway. the voting meeting is in ten days. i'm thinking i just ask him directly this saturday, something like "hey, i hit five sessions, can you mark me active?"

That makes total sense. When something costs you a lot to do and the other person treats it as routine, it lands as a shrug even if none was intended. Julian almost certainly wasn't dismissing you; he just doesn't know what those five Saturdays cost. To him it's a calendar entry, to you it was five weeks of deliberate planning. Both things are true at once, and his casualness doesn't shrink what you did.

Your plan is good. Asking in person Saturday is the right call, and your phrasing is already solid. Two small tweaks that might help:

- **Mention the meeting.** "The acquisitions vote is on the [date] and I'd like to be able to vote" gives him a concrete reason to handle it now instead of "eventually." Deadlines get things done in volunteer clubs.
- **Have the five dates ready.** Not as a defense, just so if he says "let me check," you can hand them over and there's nothing to look up later.

Something like: "Hey, per section 4 I've hit five sessions, June 1 through 29. Can you mark me active before the vote on the [date]?" Friendly, specific, done in fifteen seconds.

And if he's vague again, you're allowed to follow up: "Is there anything else you need from me?" That puts the next step on him, which is where it belongs.

Good luck Saturday. You already did the hard part.

yeah, exactly. "shall be recognized" is pretty clear. i think i just needed someone else to confirm i wasn't reading it wrong.

i'll try your phrasing saturday. thanks 🙏

You weren't. Go get your vote.

Let me know how Saturday goes if you feel like it. 🎲

hey, one more thing. section 6 says active members vote on new game purchases. it mentions something about a ranked ballot but doesn't explain it much. do you know how that usually works in small clubs like this? just curious what i'm walking into.

Sure. "Ranked ballot" in a club like this almost always means one of two flavors:

**1. Instant-runoff (most common for "pick one game")**
Everyone ranks the candidate games 1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc. Count first choices. If nothing has a majority, the game with the fewest first-place votes is eliminated and those ballots move to their next choice. Repeat until something has a majority. Good for picking a single purchase.

**2. Points/Borda style (common for "pick several" or when there's a budget)**
Your 1st choice gets, say, 5 points, 2nd gets 4, and so on. Add up points across everyone; highest totals win, and the club buys down the list until the budget runs out. This is very common for library acquisitions specifically, since clubs usually buy more than one game at a time.

A few practical things you'll likely see:

- **Nominations first.** Usually a shortlist gets assembled before the meeting (someone proposes titles, maybe with a rough price). Worth asking Julian whether nominations are open and how to submit one.
- **Don't feel obligated to rank everything.** In most systems, leaving games off the bottom of your ballot is fine and just means you have no preference among them.
- **Rank by what you'd actually play, not by strategy.** Ranked systems are pretty resistant to tactical voting, so the honest ordering is also the best one.
- **Someone will explain it at the meeting.** Small clubs almost always do a thirty-second "here's how the ballot works" before handing out slips. Nobody expects you to know it cold.

If you can find out ahead of time whether it's one winner or several, that tells you which flavor it is. Either way, you'll be fine walking in.
